rewrites.summary:
Rio de Janeiro recorded only 3 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — roughly 0.18 per million against a population near 17 million — well below the national average, so lethal violence is the weakest part of the risk picture here. The visitor-facing signals are about enforcement: a documented extortion racket in Niterói ran for about two years under the appearance of backing from public agents, and in Copacabana the tourist police arrested two trans women for extorting a visiting tourist with threats to circulate intimate videos.

Institutional response was mixed. The state court decreed preventive detention in February 2026 for the alleged extorter, an ex-employee of Niterói city hall, so the judiciary can act, and the tourist-police arrests likewise show police presence in tourist areas. Yet the Niterói scheme operated openly for roughly two years, forcing trans sex workers to pay weekly exactions, which signals weak protection for the most exposed trans residents and a tourist-area climate in which visibly trans people may be treated as scam suspects.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
National context: the 2025 national dossier logged 80 trans and travesti killings across the country, a drop of about 34% year on year, in a country that leads the world tally — the same table that supplies this state's 3-killings figure — and the national scoring baseline (0.71) is the reference for the deviation of about 0.03 below national. The deviation rests on these enforcement signals rather than on homicide. Neighbour comparison: São Paulo carries no deviation from the national figure, so its reading is the numerical norm while Rio's is qualitative.

Litigation flux: the February 2026 arrest and remand steps are current per freshness checks; later trial steps were not searchable in the sandbox and do not yet change the enforcement picture.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Trans sex workers in central Niterói reported a coercive regime running about two years: a man claiming militia and public-agent connections forced each to pay R$120 per week and threatened them, reportedly 'almost strangling three of the girls.' The alleged extorter had been an employee of Niterói city hall until January 2026, was arrested in the 'Operação Ronda Sumbria' operation by the 76ª police precinct, and was remanded in pre-trial custody.

A trans council member brought the case to the Public Ministry. The episode documents resident-facing exploitation of trans sex workers with an appearance of official involvement and a functioning if slow judicial response.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No passport, document-screening or border procedure finding specific to this state was located in the audited sources; none is known to differ from national practice. No marriage or partner-travel finding specific to this state was located. The trial outcome of the Niterói extortion case is unknown — later steps were not searchable per freshness checks, and the two documented enforcement episodes may not generalise to a statewide pattern.

rewrites.summary:
Goiás recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — a per-capita rate of about 0.69 per million per year against a population of ~7.2 million, roughly 1.8 times the national rate from that year's 80 national killings. For a trans visitor the operative risk factor is geographic: the national dossier finds most such killings occur in interior cities outside the capitals, where monitoring, reporting and access to public policy are weaker, and a visitor travelling beyond the capital shares that interior exposure.

No Goiás-specific ordinance, legal restriction or protection measure was identified in the audited sources; the risk profile therefore rests on the above-national per-capita killing count and the interior-concentration pattern rather than on any local legal hostility.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
National context: the 2025 dossier counted 80 trans and travesti killings across the country (~211 million people), and the companion 2024 dossier recorded 122 killings, 16% below 2023 — the national trend is falling year on year in a country that leads the world tally. The same interior-concentration statistic (~68% outside capitals) appears in both years' dossiers.

Maranhão and Pará, the two neighbouring states whose 5-killings figure matched this one for 2025, place Goiás in the national mid-band rather than at either extreme.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing data: the dossier attributes the interior exposure to weaker monitoring, reporting and access to public policy outside the capitals, reporting that 67.5% of national killings in 2025 — and roughly 68% in 2024 — occurred there. Interior trans residents are therefore both more exposed and less able to rely on public monitoring and policy access.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No Goiás-specific ordinance, legal restriction or protection measure was identified in the audited sources; the risk profile rests on the national dossier counts alone. No qualitative incident, court or enforcement finding specific to this state was located. National-level policy developments that could change documents, screening or enforcement for trans visitors are not documented in this record and remain unresolved.

rewrites.summary:
Alagoas recorded 6 killings of trans and travesti people in 2024 — among the elevated small-state totals in that year's dossier table — and just 2 in 2025. No Alagoas-specific legal restriction or enforcement finding is documented; the national framework applies uniformly.

The swing between consecutive dossiers on a small population is itself the visitor-relevant finding: at these denominators a couple of cases moves the state's position sharply, and the monitoring body cautions that falling national counts partly reflect violence shifting into attempted homicides rather than improving safety. Places the risk wherever a visibly trans person is in public: the dossiers' regional victim profile — young, Black, poor, killed in public places at night — makes open visibility the operative hazard, and the state sits inside the country's hardest-hit region.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The national trajectory frames the reading: 80 killings in 2025 (a ~34% year-on-year fall) after 122 in 2024 (16% below 2023), with the monitoring body reporting the counts fall while the violence shifts form — attempted homicides taking over from completed ones. This state's 6-to-2 swing is a small-denominator artefact within that falling national picture rather than an independent improvement.

rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The monitoring body's caution is a data caveat: persistent under-recording, including misclassification of victims' gender identity, degrades the counts, and falling national figures partly reflect violence shifting into attempted homicides. rewrites.summary:
Mato Grosso recorded 3 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — about 0.83 per million per year, more than double the national rate — after the 2024 dossier counted 8 killings in the state, its highest year. The dossier's finding that most killings happen outside the capitals makes small-town exposure relevant for visitors travelling beyond the capital, so the elevated per-capita reading is the core of the assessment even though three cases on a small population are statistically fragile.

On documents and institutional response, two local positives exist: a 2021 decree guarantees the social-name right, accepted by state public offices and usable on badges, cards and identification documents, and a 2026 jury conviction of 13 years and 6 months for the gender-motivated killing of a trans woman shows the courts can deliver. No trans-specific ordinance or protection beyond these was found; the national framework applies uniformly.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The national dossier frames the reading: 80 killings nationally in 2025 (a ~34% fall), 1,261 killings recorded over 2017-2025, and at least 75 attempted homicides in 2025; the state ranked 12th among the country's states in 2025 and has recorded 43 killings of trans and gender-diverse people since 2017. The dossier's interior-concentration finding (67.5% of killings outside capitals) is the mechanism connecting the national pattern to small-town risk here.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Resident-facing facts: the March 2021 decree requires state public offices to accept the social name, lets it appear on badges, cards and identification documents, lets state employees register the social name in internal records and systems, and forbids official publications from using the civil name without consent — an administrative-recognition practice for residents.

Resident discrimination and enforcement data: the dossier records 43 killings of travestis, trans women and other trans people in this state since 2017, and a jury in April 2026 convicted a businessman of the feminicide of a trans woman, explicitly holding the killing motivated by gender-based contempt and discrimination, in a 13-years-and-6-months sentence.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Three cases on a small population is statistically fragile, and no other qualitative incident, ordinance or enforcement pattern beyond the dossier counts and the single conviction was found. No border-screening, passport or entry-document finding specific to this state was located. No marriage or partner-travel finding specific to this state was located. The degree to which public offices actually comply with the social-name decree is not documented in the audited sources.

Lists this state/province at 3 killings for 2025.

A January 2026 report: this state/province has recorded 43 killings of trans women and other trans people since 2017, against a national total of 80 in 2025. A state/province-specific reading of the same national dossier the summary cites for the 3 killings in 2025.

An April 2026 report: a businessman was sentenced by a jury to 13 years and 6 months in prison for the feminicide of a trans woman — found dead with knife wounds in January 2024 — with the jury holding the killing was motivated by gender-based contempt and discrimination. A documented state/province conviction that explicitly recognizes the gender dimension of a trans woman's killing.

A March 2021 report: a decree published in the state/province's official gazette guarantees trans people the right to use their social name, accepted by state/province public offices and usable on badges, cards and identification documents; employees can register the social name in internal records, and official publications may not use the civil name without consent. An identified state/province measure recognizing trans identity, relevant to documents and name usage within the state/province.

rewrites.summary:
The Comunitat Valenciana holds both a dedicated integral law on the right to gender identity and expression and a general LGTBI-equality statute — one of only three communities to legislate in both the trans-specific and general-LGTBI categories — and, unlike the peer community that shares the dual structure, it has not amended or narrowed its provisions. The statutory framework supports institutional response channels for a visitor encountering discrimination.

Enforcement evidence is thin but positive: a documented conviction in the community's court system — six months' prison, suspended, plus fines and a moral-damages payment — for chasing, insulting and recording a trans woman solely because of her gender identity shows the institutional response channel for discrimination operates. No negative visitor-facing finding, incident pattern or enforcement gap was located in the research pass, and the capital carries a visible, well-established LGTBI community with dedicated infrastructure.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National calibration: the assessment deviates +0.03 above the national figure (0.88) on the strength of the dual-category framework being active and unrevised. Neighbour comparisons: the peer community sharing the dual structure (0.83) actively rolled back its provisions in 2023, making the Valencian position clearly safer on that axis; a neighbouring community with no such law at all (0.81) sits 0.10 points below on the presence-versus-absence of statutory infrastructure. An educational-policy survey groups this community with four others among the leaders on coverage.
rewrites.localsOnly: The regional identity-and-expression law's registry and administrative procedures operate for residents; a visitor never invokes them. Under it, public bodies of the community must treat people according to their felt gender identity, and the law provides for administrative documentation and an advice-and-support service for trans people and their families — a resident-facing administrative recognition practice.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No incident data, enforcement action or negative visitor-facing finding beyond the single documented conviction was located for this community in the research pass; the assessment rests on statutory completeness and that one enforcement outcome. No border-screening, passport, documents or marriage/partner-travel finding specific to this community was located. The applicability of the community's laws to a visiting trans person rather than a resident is not separately tested in the audited sources.

A national LGTBI federation's 2025 survey of public educational policies across the country's regions tracks which have gender-identity protocols and education legislation; it notes this state/province's elected local legislature completing its gender legislation and groups it with several other communities among the leaders on educational policy coverage.

Official gazette text of the state/province's April 2017 law on the integral recognition of the right to gender identity and expression: its first article makes the law's purpose the guarantee of an adequate normative framework for gender self-determination for people whose felt gender identity differs from that assigned at birth; public bodies of the state/province must treat people according to their felt gender identity; and a later title provides for administrative documentation and an advice-and-support service for trans people and their families. Primary legal text confirming the dedicated integral law this record cites, enacted 7 April 2017.

Official gazette text of the state/province's November 2018 equality law for LGTBI people: provisions cover non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity/expression, access and admission rights, reversal of the burden of proof, and a regime of administrative infringements and sanctions for discrimination against LGTBI people. Primary legal text confirming the general-equality-statute category alongside the 2017 trans-specific law — the dual-category framework on which this record's assessment rests.

A report of a conviction by the regional court in a city over a June 2022 park incident: an adult with several minors insulted, chased, recorded and mocked a trans woman solely because of her gender identity. The adult accepted six months' prison, suspended on condition of committing no offence for two years, plus a fine and a moral-damages indemnity to the victim; two minors had already been sentenced to supervision measures, and a hate-crime prosecutor handled the case. Documents an institutional response channel operating in the community: a gender-identity-motivated offence investigated, charged and resulting in a sentence.

rewrites.summary:
Buenos Aires Province carries the strongest sub-national negative signal in the country: the provincial human-rights ombudsman's 2016 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents acts of violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police — or by third parties under police cover — against trans and travesti people during operations in three cities (La Plata, Mar del Plata and Esteban Echeverría), under 'preventive policing' frameworks. Academic legal analysis confirms that after the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence, security forces increased use of drug-law prosecution — devolved to provincial justice in 2005 — and street-offence law as the operative instrument of indirect criminalisation of travesti/trans identity: a patterned, state-implicated escalation.

For a trans visitor the operative risk is arbitrary detention during any police stop. The evidence is not a single incident but a documented operational framework that measurably increased police persecution of trans women, and the protective institutions that coexist — the provincial ombudsman's 2024 registry-rectification guide and its discrimination-caseload machinery — are resident-facing and do not offset that exposure. No provincial law criminalises gender identity; enforcement practice, not statute, does the work.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
National context: the deviation from the national figure (0.58) is negative (-0.05), no other province has a comparable volume of multi-source, patterned enforcement documentation reaching the UN treaty-body system, and compared with the silent majority of provinces the difference is one of documented pattern rather than statutory hostility. Peer comparison: the autonomous capital (0.55) keeps a tribunal-based judicial-oversight structure and an anti-discrimination apparatus that the province lacks, and this province's police-judge model under its minor-offences code gives less post-detention review.

Parent-country policy turbulence: a December 2024 national decree added consent and medical-judicial requirements for minors' gender-affirming care, currently under litigation; the 2012 national Gender Identity Law remains in force, and the autonomous capital keeps its protective local framework.
rewrites.localsOnly: The provincial ombudsman's 2024 registry-rectification guide covers gender-marker rectification for people born in the province, including people now living elsewhere, and its discrimination-caseload machinery documents resident discrimination cases. These serve residents; a visitor never uses them.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The 2016-17 UN-review documents are dated: they do not describe current law, and whether the documented police pattern persists at the same intensity today cannot be re-verified from the audited sources. The litigation over the December 2024 national decree remains unresolved. No border-screening, passport, documents or marriage/partner-travel finding specific to this province was located.
